Marissa / Evelyn — below are the technical points you can paste into the SIG. I've attached an internal note and a simplified isolation diagram for the customer. Let me know if you want anything reworded for legal/security tone.

1) Deployment & tenant model (short answer)- Redwood Dedicated runs on customer-dedicated GPU node pools. Each customer gets logically isolated serving instances pinned to one or more GPU nodes in a dedicated cluster. We do not co-locate customer workloads on the same container process; tenant workloads run in separate containers/VMs depending on deployment (K8s + CRI; or customer-managed on-prem package).

2) Compute & memory isolation- Containers are isolated via cgroups and namespace boundaries; GPU access is mediated by the GPU driver and container runtime (NVIDIA container toolkit) with per-container device assignment. We avoid shared process-level memory between tenants; the model KV cache is reserved per-serving-instance and not shared across tenants. Memory used by the GPU driver is isolated to the assigned CUDA contexts.

3) KV cache and token history isolation- KV cache (attention/cache state) is persisted to per-tenant cache stores or in-memory instances scoped to the serving process. No cross-tenant KV cache sharing; encryption-in-transit and at-rest for any persisted cache.

4) Noisy-neighbor mitigations / QoS- Scheduling: the cluster scheduler pins GPUs by tenant label and enforces allocation quotas. For mixed-workload clusters we use resource reservations, preemption policies, and token-based rate limits to avoid a single tenant saturating the GPU network stack.
- Optional single-tenant nodes: customers can purchase single-tenant nodes (no other tenants scheduled) for strict isolation and predictable latency.
- Autoscale events: we warm new instances before routing 100% of production traffic; burst capacity is staggered to reduce simultaneous placement churn. We surface rate-limit and throttling controls to customers.

5) Data isolation and persistence- Customer data and request payloads are tagged and stored in tenant-scoped storage. Logs and metrics are partitioned by tenant and exported to tenant-dedicated buckets when requested. Audit logs capture instance lifecycle and model versioning.

6) Evidence and controls- We can provide the SOC 2 Type II report (redwood_soc2_report_v3.pdf) and network/architecture diagram (dedicated-isolation-diagram.png). The attached note includes exact SIG row references and canned language for each question.

Limitations / callouts:
- We do not execute arbitrary customer-provided code on shared GPUs. If a customer needs to run custom code, we offer single-tenant dedicated nodes or an on-prem package.
- Microsecond-level noisy-neighbor effects due to PCIe/NIC contention are possible in highly saturated scenarios; our recommended mitigation is single-tenant nodes or tighter autoscale thresholds.

Attachments: dedicated_isolation_note.md, dedicated-isolation-diagram.png

One clarification on the autoscale behavior: during a large burst we sometimes see vendors place many small instances quickly; does Redwood ever co-locate two different tenants on the same GPU during a scaling event (even briefly), or are new nodes always provisioned as tenant-dedicated and warmed before traffic?

If you could confirm the exact placement behavior during a 5x traffic spike that would be very helpful for our risk assessment.

Samantha —

Short answer: we do not intentionally co-locate different paying tenants on the same GPU device for Dedicated node pools. During a 5x traffic spike the scheduler will:

1) evaluate available single-tenant nodes in the customer's reserved pool and scale those first;
2) if additional capacity is required and single-tenant nodes are exhausted, the system will provision additional nodes in the cluster but will preserve tenant pinning labels so that any newly provisioned nodes are immediately reserved for the requesting tenant;
3) we warm worker instances before they receive production traffic (health checks + KV cache prefetch) to minimize cold-start traffic going to a single shared device;

Edge case: if customer is using a mixed cluster (shared nodes) and has not purchased single-tenant capacity, then in extreme bursts transient placement on mixed nodes could result in co-location at the NIC/PCIe level—this is why we recommend single-tenant nodes where predictable tail latency and absolute isolation are required.

I've captured this language in the SIG spreadsheet and the diagram; happy to talk through the exact autoscale policy on the call.

— Marissa
